question.problem: If the fifth term of a geometric sequence is $\frac{1}{8}$ and the common ratio is $\frac{1}{4},$ then the eighth term of this sequence is{{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:
The common ratio is $r=\frac{1}{4},$ so we can start writing the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we still need to figure out the first term ${a}_{1}.$ We know that the $5$th term is ${a}_{5}=\frac{1}{8},$ so we can solve for the first term as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{5} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{5-1} \\ \frac{1}{8} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{4} \\ \frac{1}{8} & ={a}_{1}\cdot (\frac{1}{256}) \\ \frac{256}{8} & ={a}_{1} \\ 32 & ={a}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the first term is ${a}_{1}=32,$ we can complete the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n-1} \\  & =32\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can use this formula to compute the $8$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{8} & =32\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{8-1} \\  & =32\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{7} \\  & ={2}^{5}\cdot \frac{1}{{4}^{7}} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{5}}{({2}^{2})^{7}} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{5}}{{2}^{14}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{2}^{9}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $8$th term is ${a}_{8}=\frac{1}{{2}^{9}}.$
